cards.text: Saul, Israel's king, is dead. David, the man Samuel anointed to be the next king (1 Samuel 16:13), just got back from defeating the Amalekites and has been in Ziklag two days. On the third day, a man walks in from Saul's camp with his clothes torn and dust on his head.

cards.question: When the man from Saul's camp reaches David, he falls to the ground to pay him homage.

cards.text: David asks where he's coming from, and the man says he escaped from the Israelite camp. Then David asks, "What was the outcome?" and I bet his heart is POUNDING.

cards.question: The man tells David the troops fled from the battle. What does he say happened to Saul and his son Jonathan?

cards.text: David doesn't just take his word for it. He asks how he KNOWS Saul and Jonathan are dead, the same way you ask "Says who?" when the group chat swears the boss quit.

The man says he happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and the cavalry closing in. Saul turned, saw him and called out, and he answered, "Here I am!"

cards.question: The man says Saul asked him who he was. What does the man say he told Saul?
The man says Saul, in agony with chariots closing in, begged him to stand over him and ___ him.

cards.text: The man says he stood over Saul and killed him, because he knew that after Saul had fallen he couldn't survive. Then he says he took something off Saul to bring to David.

cards.question: The man says he took two things from Saul and brought them to David. What are they?

cards.text: Hold up. Back in 1 Samuel 31:4, Saul took his own sword and fell on it, so this man's story doesn't match.

cards.question: When David hears the news, he and all his men take hold of their own ___ and tear them.
David and his men mourn and weep and fast until evening, but only for Saul and Jonathan.

cards.text: Then David asks the young man where he's from, and he says, "I am the son of a foreigner," an Amalekite. Friend, the same Amalekites David JUST got back from fighting!

cards.question: David has a question for the Amalekite who says he killed Saul. What does David ask him?

answers.text: Why he wasn't afraid to destroy the LORD's anointed
Why he didn't bring Jonathan's body back home
Why he came all alone to the camp at Ziklag

cards.question: Then David summons one of his young men and tells him to ___ the Amalekite.

cards.text: David had told him, "Your blood be on your own head because your own mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I killed the LORD’s anointed.’" His own words decided it.
Then David takes up a lament, a song of grief, for Saul and his son Jonathan. And he gives an order about it.

cards.question: David orders that his lament for Saul and Jonathan, the Song of the Bow, be taught. Who is supposed to learn it?
David's Song of the Bow is written in the Book of ___.

cards.text: The song opens with Israel's glory lying slain on the heights. Then comes a line David keeps coming back to: "How the mighty have fallen!"
Next David names two Philistine cities. He says, "Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon."

cards.question: Why doesn't David want the news of Saul's death told in Gath and Ashkelon?

answers.text: So no one comes after Judah
So Israel can hear it first

cards.text: Nobody wants the rival team's fans hearing about the big loss. Then David speaks to the mountains of Gilboa: may they have no dew or rain, no fields yielding offerings of grain.

cards.question: David says that on Gilboa, the ___ of Saul was defiled.

cards.text: Then David remembers Saul and Jonathan in battle. He sings that the bow of Jonathan did not retreat.

cards.question: In David's song, the sword of Saul did not return empty.
David calls Saul and Jonathan beloved and delightful in life. What does he say about them in death?

cards.text: David says they were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions, and this is the same Saul who searched for David every day (1 Samuel 23:14). Me? Somebody slid me into a junk drawer once and I gave up on myself for YEARS.
Then David calls on the daughters of Israel to weep for Saul.

cards.question: Why does David say the daughters of Israel should weep for Saul?

answers.text: He dressed them in scarlet and gold
He gave them homes in the hills
He sang songs in their honor

cards.text: David comes back to that line, "How the mighty have fallen," and then turns to Jonathan. Jonathan, Saul's son, loved David as himself (1 Samuel 18:1).

cards.question: Speaking straight to Jonathan, David grieves for him and calls him my ___.
David says Jonathan's love to him was extraordinary.

cards.text: David closes with that line one more time: "How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!" And that's where we leave it for now, friend, because this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 5 quotes "Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Card 1 opens with "Saul, Israel's king, is dead." Card 4 then asks what the man says happened to Saul and Jonathan. Because the baker already knows Saul is dead, 'They were taken captive' and 'They fled across the Jordan' are ruled out before the question is asked. Card 1 needs reworking (for example, opening with David back in Ziklag and the man arriving, without stating the outcome), or card 4 needs to ask something card 1 hasn't settled.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Card 1's setup line rules out the wrong answers on card 4, since Saul's death is already stated.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This story card tells only 1 Samuel 31:4, which is outside the passage. It doesn't move the baker through 2 Samuel 1. It also claims the man's story 'doesn't match,' which settles how the two accounts connect when the passage itself never says the Amalekite lied.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: Saying the man's story 'doesn't match' decides a connection between the two passages that 2 Samuel 1 leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "The same Amalekites David JUST got back from fighting" says this man belongs to the group David fought in verse 1. The text only says he is an Amalekite. It never ties him to that raid.

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true. "Same words" means an exact match.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Why he wasn't afraid to destroy the LORD's anointed,' uses the passage's own phrase. The wrong answers are plain modern wording, so the right one stands out as more like the Bible. Also, 'the camp at Ziklag' calls the town a camp.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The execution in verse 15b ('So the young man struck him down, and he died') is never told. Card 16 asks only about David's order, and card 17 moves to verse 16 with 'His own words decided it,' so the baker never actually hears that the Amalekite died.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The card spends words defining 'lament' ('a song of grief').

rule.text: Don't spend card words explaining a hard word. Hard words get a dictionary pop-up (definitions.md, made after the cards).

findings.problem: 'Book of ___' (Jashar) tests a name the baker hasn't seen and can't reason out. It isn't a word that carries the passage's meaning. It also comes right after another discovery question (card 2).

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card's opening joke is about verse 20 (not wanting the enemy to hear), but the card cites only 2 Samuel 1:21.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: 'the ___ of Saul was defiled' asks the baker to guess a word in a line of the song (shield, crown or spear). Nothing earlier lets them reason it out. This is the same kind of detail guess as the oil example.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The joke compares David praising the man who hunted him to Papa Dorin giving up on himself in the drawer. Those aren't the same action (honoring someone who wronged you versus giving up on yourself), so the punchline doesn't click.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The 'story isn't over' line nearly copies the doc's example ('And that's where we'll leave it for now. Trust me, friend, this story's not done.').

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: Across both stops, the humor is thin. Most cards read as plain retelling, and only a few have a comparison, and none of those lands as a real laugh. A grief passage calls for restraint, but there are still moments, like David's caution in verse 5 or the man's convenient story, that could hold a stronger laugh without muddying a fact.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
